A run produces results: for each disease, the number of people in each state at each time point, and the number who made each transition in each step, plus any other quantities the model declares (prevalence, reported cases). This page covers what the results are, how to read them, how to change their time step, split them by group, compare them with data, summarize and export them, and plot them. Results know what they are (their labels, their time points, whether they are counts or shares, and any data they are compared with), so most plots take one line; the second half of the page covers plotting a sim, a module, and a single result; comparing scenarios and many runs; choosing what to plot; styles and fonts; saving figures; and falling back to Matplotlib for anything else.

## Where results are

After a run, `sim.results` holds the results of each module by name, and the sim's own (such as `alive`, the population size):

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=10)) # 90% immune, 10 infectious

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()

res = sim.results.measles
print(res)
```

## R

```r
library(starsim)

states("S I R")
measles <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I), # β = 1.9 per day
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),  # Infectious for 8 days on average
  init   = list(R = 0.9), # 90% immune
  init_n = list(I = 10)   # 10 infectious
)

sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2025-07-01", verbose = 0)
sim$run()

res <- sim$results$measles
res
```
:::

A disease has a result for each state (`S`, `I`, `R`: the number of people in it at each time point) and each transition (`infection`, `recovery`: the number who made it during each step), named after the variables they were made from. `res.I` and `res['I']` are the same. A disease with transmission also has `infected` and `prevalence`, added by Starsim; [Names with special meaning](building_diseases.qmd#names-with-special-meaning) lists the results every disease gets.

The sim's own results are those of the people: `alive`, `died`, and `emigrated` (and, as agents, `female`), each step. `record_people=False` on the sim skips them, which saves a little time in a light model that doesn't need them (demographics read `alive`).

## Reading a result

Each result is an `ss.Result`. It behaves like a NumPy array, one number per time point (so you can index, slice, and do arithmetic on it directly), but it also carries what it is:

| Attribute | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| `values` | The NumPy array of values |
| `timevec` | The time point of each value |
| `label` | A human-readable label, used in plots |
| `kind` | What kind of quantity it is: a stock, a flow, or a ratio (below) |
| `scale` | Whether the result is a count that scales with the population (as agents, each agent stands for some number of people); by default, a flow or stock does and a ratio doesn't |
| `low`, `high` | Bounds, for a result that has them |

```{python}
print('Peak infectious:', round(res.I.max()))
print('Total infections:', round(res.infection.sum()))
print('Infectious at the end:', round(res.I[-1]))
print('First time points:', res.I.timevec[:3])
```

Each result says what kind of quantity it is, as its `kind`, which decides how it is added up over time (its `summarize_by`), whether it has a running total, and how it is compared with data:

| `kind` | `summarize_by` | What it is | Examples | Over a period |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `'stock'` | `'last'` | A number at each time point | `S`, `I`, `R` | Resampled, the value at the start (a running total, `.cum`, at the end); over the whole run, the last value |
| `'flow'` | `'sum'` | A number of events during each step | `infection`, `recovery`, `cases` | The total |
| `'ratio'` | `'mean'` | One number divided by another | `prevalence` | Worked out again from the totals of its parts (the mean, for one with no parts) |

A result of your own gives it as `ss.Result('protected', kind='stock')`. The name can say it instead (`new_...` is a flow, `n_...` and `cum_...` are stocks, and a name ending in `prevalence` is a ratio); with neither, `ss.Result('doses')` is taken as a flow if its type is an integer and as a ratio otherwise, with a warning, so give `kind=`. The kind also says whether the result is scaled by the number of people each agent stands for: a flow or stock is, and a ratio isn't (`scale=` overrides this). `kind=None` is for a result with no meaning over time, which isn't summarized. To summarize a result another way without changing what it is, give `summarize_by=` too: `ss.Result('new_cases', kind='flow', summarize_by='mean')` is a flow (it still has a running total, and is summed to compare it with weekly data) whose summary over the run is its mean per step.

A flow's running total is `.cum`, so `res.infection.cum[-1]` is the number of infections over the whole run. Two cautions: summing a stock over time does not count people (`res.I.sum()` counts each person once for every step they are infectious), and the people infectious at the start are not new infections during the run, so `infection.sum()` leaves them out; add them if your definition of outbreak size includes everyone ever infected.

### Time points

A result has one value for each time point of the sim, from `start` to `stop`, and a step is taken from each, the last included, so each time point is a period: the step that starts there. `I[0]` is the number infectious at the start, and `infection[0]` is the number of infections during the first step. A flow is dated by the start of its step: with daily steps, the infections dated 1 January are those during 1 January. The state after the last step is not recorded, so after a run, `sim.people` is one step past the last time point of the results.

```{python}
print('Infectious at the start:', res.I[0])
print('Infections in the first step:', round(res.infection[0], 2))
print('Infectious after the first step:', round(res.I[1], 2))
```

## More results: ratios and outcomes

A model can declare more results. A ratio of states, such as prevalence, is given to the disease along with the transitions, and an outcome (`ss.outcome()`) is a quantity worked out from flows, such as the cases that are reported: here, half of infections, three days after they happen:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
N = S + I + R
infection  = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery   = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
prevalence = I / N                                   # The share of people infectious
cases      = ss.outcome(0.5*infection, delay=ss.days(3)) # Half of infections are reported, 3 days later
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, prevalence, cases, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=10))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.measles
sim.plot('measles')
```

## R

```r
states("S I R")
N <- S + I + R
infection <- Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I)
measles <- Disease(
  infection  = infection,
  recovery   = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),
  prevalence = I / N,                                     # The share of people infectious
  cases      = outcome(0.5 * infection, delay = days(3)), # Half of infections are reported, 3 days later
  init   = list(R = 0.9),
  init_n = list(I = 10)
)

sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2025-07-01", verbose = 0)
sim$run()
res <- sim$results$measles
sim$plot("measles")
```
:::

Each result is named after its variable (`prevalence`, `cases`). See [Outcomes](building_outcomes.qmd) for reporting, delays, and how long people stay in an outcome such as hospital.

## Changing the time step of a result

`resample()` gives a result over longer periods (`'day'`, `'week'`, `'month'`, `'year'`, or a duration such as `ss.weeks(2)`), adding it up by its `summarize_by` without being told: weekly cases are the total over each week, monthly numbers infectious are the value at the start of each month, and a running total (`.cum`) is the value at the end of each period. Each period is labeled by its start (1 January for a year, the 1st for a month, otherwise its first time point). `to_series()` gives a pandas series with the dates as its index:

```{python}
res.cases.resample('week').to_series().head()
```

```{python}
res.I.resample('month').to_series()
```

## Results by group

A disease stratified by age (see [Stratification](building_stratification.qmd)) still has one result for each state and transition; each is the total over the groups, and has the groups inside it. `select()` picks groups, and `by()` gives one line for each. Here the measles model is stratified by age, with the contact matrix of [Stratification](building_stratification.qmd#age-groups-and-contacts), in which children have the most contacts; with contacts, β is per contact, so it is given its value per contact by name:

```{python}
by_age = measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}, inplace=False) # A stratified copy
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]])
sim = ss.Sim(by_age, networks=contacts, pars=dict(beta=0.14), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()

res = sim.results.measles
print('Peak infectious, all ages:', round(res.I.max()))
print('Peak infectious, aged 0-14:', round(res.I.select(age='0-14').max()))
res.prevalence.by('age').plot()
```

The share of children infectious peaks earlier and higher than among adults, since children meet the most people. (Adults and people 65 and over have the same number of contacts in all, 12 a day, so their lines lie on top of each other.) A ratio such as prevalence is never averaged over groups: its numerator and denominator are each added up over the groups selected, and then divided.

A module written as code can keep its results by group too, rather than one result for each group (`prevalence_f_15_20` and so on). Stratify the sim, make the result with `groups=True`, and set it at each step from `sim.groups.count()`, which counts the people alive in each group for whom a condition holds, in one pass. As agents, stratifying by a property people already have, such as sex or age, changes nothing in the run, so it can be done for the results alone:

```{python}
class ByGroup(ss.Analyzer):
    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(ss.Result('prevalence', groups=True))

    def record_stocks(self): # At the start of each step, as the other stocks are
        super().record_stocks()
        groups = self.sim.groups
        self.results.prevalence.set_groups(self.ti, groups.count(self.sim.diseases.sis.I), groups.count()) # The infected over everyone, in each group

sim = ss.Sim(ss.SIS(), networks='random', analyzers=ByGroup(), stratify=dict(sex=['female', 'male'], age=[0, 15, 50]), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.bygroup.prevalence.select(sex='female', age='15-49').plot()
```

Nothing in this SIS model depends on sex or age, so the prevalence among women aged 15–49 is the same as in anyone else, but for chance; the example shows the mechanics, which are the same for a model in which they differ.

## Results with several columns

Sometimes a result naturally has several values at each time point, such as new infections by variant or by age group. For a declared disease, [stratifying](#results-by-group) does this. In a module written as code, rather than defining one result per group, give `columns=` to `ss.Result`, which makes a result with a column for each. Here an analyzer counts new infections among children and adults separately:

```{python}
import numpy as np

class InfectionsByAge(ss.Analyzer):
    """ Count new infections among children and adults """
    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('new_infections', columns=['children', 'adults'], label='New infections'),
        )

    def step(self):
        new = self.sim.diseases.sis.infection.uids # Those infected in this step
        children = self.sim.people.age[new] < 15
        self.results.new_infections[self.ti] = [np.count_nonzero(children), np.count_nonzero(~children)]

sim = ss.Sim(ss.SIS(), networks='random', analyzers=InfectionsByAge(), n_agents=2000, start='2000-01-01', stop='2000-12-31', verbose=0)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.infectionsbyage.new_infections
print('Shape:', res.shape)
print('Columns:', res.columns)
```

Each column is available as a result of its own, as `res.adults`, `res['adults']`, or `res.select(column='adults')`. These share their data with the whole result, so changing one changes the other. Most operations handle each column separately: they are scaled by the number of people each agent stands for, `to_df()` gives one column of the table each, `sim.summarize()` summarizes each, and `resample()` sums each over the period (since this result is a flow):

```{python}
monthly = res.resample('month')
monthly.to_df().head()
```

Plotting the result shows one line per column:

```{python}
res.plot()
```

## Comparing with data

Data is matched to results by name: a column called `cases` in a table given as `data=` is compared with the result `cases`, and plotted with it, and weekly data is compared with the total of a flow over each week. [Outcomes](building_outcomes.qmd#data-attached-by-name) covers attaching data, including making data from a run of the model with `sim.to_synthetic_data()`; it is the data that [calibration](calibration_fitting.qmd) fits to.

## Summaries and export

`sim.summarize()` gives each result over the whole run, by its `summarize_by`: the total of a flow (`'sum'`), the final value of a stock (`'last'`), and the mean of a ratio (`'mean'`). It is a table with a row for each result and one column, `value`, as `msim.summarize()` gives for many runs (see below), so one run and many read the same way; results that are 0 throughout are kept, so the tables of different runs line up row for row. `sim.summarize('measles_infection')` gives one result's summary as a number, and `how=` summarizes another way, e.g. `sim.summarize('measles_I', how='max')` for the peak (`how=` takes `'mean'`, `'median'`, `'sum'`, `'last'`, `'max'`, `'min'`, or a function).

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0) # The measles model with prevalence and reported cases, not stratified
sim.run()
sim.summarize()
```

## R

```r
sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2025-07-01", verbose = 0)
sim$run()
summary(sim) # As sim$summarize(), as a named vector
```
:::

`to_df()` gives results as a table (a pandas dataframe), for one module or for the whole sim, with one column per result; it can then be saved with `df.to_csv()` or `df.to_excel()`:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
df = sim.to_df()
df.head()
```

## R

```r
df <- as.data.frame(sim) # As sim$to_df(), as an R data frame
head(df)
```
:::

A single module's results, or a single result, give a table the same way: `sim.results.measles.to_df()`, or `res.I.to_df()`. `sim.results.flatten()` gives the same results as a flat dict, keyed like the columns (`measles_I`).

## Results of many runs

The runs of a stochastic model together (see [Scenarios](running_scenarios.qmd)) have the same results as one run, with every run inside each. The usual summaries are built in:

```{python}
msim = ss.parallel(sim.new(solver='binomial'), n_runs=20)
res = msim.results.measles.I

median = res.median()            # The median of the runs at each time point
low, mid, high = res.quantiles() # The 2.5%, 50%, and 97.5% quantiles at each time point
first = res.select(run=0)        # One run
res.plot()                       # The median, and the range of 95% of the runs
```

A result of many runs knows its runs: `res.take([0, 1])` keeps some of them, `res.scenarios()` gives the positions of the runs of each scenario, and `res.axes()` its dimensions (the runs, the groups) and their levels. `res.diff('baseline')` is the difference of each other scenario from the one labeled `'baseline'`, run by run (such as the infections a vaccine averted), and `msim.diff('baseline')` the same for every result; see [Scenarios](running_scenarios.qmd).

`msim.summarize()` gives the median and interval of each result over the whole run (the total infections of each run, for example), which is not the same as the median at each time point: the quantiles at each time point summarize the runs time point by time point, so they don't give the quantiles of the epidemic's peak or of its total size.

## Plotting a sim

The plots below use the measles model above, with prevalence, written as a function of the share of people already immune so that scenarios can be compared later. With 90% immune, the outbreak is slow enough to see its shape:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
def make_measles(immune=0.9):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
    prevalence = I/(S + I + R)        # The share of people infectious
    return ss.Disease(infection, recovery, prevalence, init=dict(R=immune), init_n=dict(I=10), name='measles')

sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.plot()
```

## R

```r
make_measles <- function(immune = 0.9) {
  states("S I R")
  Disease(
    infection  = Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I), # β = 1.9 per day
    recovery   = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),  # Infectious for 8 days on average
    prevalence = I / (S + I + R),                  # The share of people infectious
    init   = list(R = immune),
    init_n = list(I = 10),
    name = "measles"
  )
}

sim <- Sim(make_measles(), total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2025-07-01", verbose = 0)
sim$run()
plot(sim) # The same as sim$plot()
```
:::

`sim.plot()` plots every result that is plotted by default, each in axes of its own, labeled and dated from the results. The sim's own results that never change (such as the number alive, in a model with no births or deaths) are left out; `show_skipped=True` includes them, and any result whose `auto_plot` is False.

What to plot is given by name, as the first argument:

| Argument | Plots |
|---|---|
| None (the default) | Every result plotted by default, each in its own axes |
| `'measles'` | The results of one module |
| `'measles.I'` (or `'measles_I'`) | One result |
| `['measles.I', 'measles.infection']` | Exactly these results, each in its own axes |
| `[['measles.S', 'measles.I', 'measles.R'], 'measles.infection']` | The results in an inner list together in one axes, with a legend |

A name that matches no result is an error that lists the names there are. Put together only results that are the same kind of quantity on a similar scale. Here the two flows, infections and recoveries (people per day), share one axes, and the number infectious (a stock: people) has its own:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
sim.plot([['measles.infection', 'measles.recovery'], 'measles.I'], figsize=(8, 6))
```

## R

```r
sim$plot(list(list("measles.infection", "measles.recovery"), "measles.I"), figsize = c(8, 6)) # A list in a list: together in one axes
```
:::

New infections rise above recoveries while the outbreak grows, and fall below them once it is past its peak, which is when the number infectious is highest.

A module plots its own results with `plot()`, which by default puts its states together in one axes: `'states'` (the default), `'flows'` (each transition's flow, in axes of its own), `'all'`, or the names of results, each argument in its own axes and a list of names together:

```{python}
sim.diseases.measles.plot('I', 'prevalence') # Two axes: the number and the share infectious
```

A model run over years can be plotted as yearly values with `annualize=True`, which adds up each result by its kind: the total of a flow over each year, the value of a stock at its start (of a running total, `.cum`, at its end), and a ratio worked out again from its parts. If the sim has data (see [Outcomes](building_outcomes.qmd#data-attached-by-name)), `sim.plot()` shows it as points with the result of the same name, with a flow summed over each period of the data, as a fit compares them, and the title says so (e.g. "weekly totals, as in the data"); `show_data=False` leaves it out.

## Plotting results

A single result plots itself, with its label as the title:

```{python}
res = sim.results.measles
res.infection.resample('week').plot() # New infections in each week
```

The same goes for anything made from a result: a result resampled to weeks or months (`resample()`), one group of a stratified result (`select(age='0-14')`), and one series per group (`by('age')`), which plots every group in one axes with a legend. A result with several columns plots one line per column. See [Changing the time step of a result](#changing-the-time-step-of-a-result), [Results by group](#results-by-group), and [Results with several columns](#results-with-several-columns) for these.

Each plotting function takes the common Matplotlib settings by name, and passes them on to the right place: `color`, `lw` (line width), `ls` (line style), `alpha`, and `marker` for the lines; `figsize` and `dpi` for the figure; `font` and `fontsize` for the text; and `data_color`, `data_size`, and `data_alpha` for the data points. Anything else can be given as a dict: `plot_kw=` is passed to `plt.plot()`, `fig_kw=` to `plt.figure()`, `data_kw=` to `plt.scatter()`, and `legend` settings such as `loc`. A setting that isn't recognized is an error listing the valid ones.

```{python}
res.I.plot(color='k', lw=3, figsize=(6, 3))
```

## Comparing scenarios and runs

Sims run together, with `ss.parallel()` or `ss.MultiSim`, plot together: each result is one axes, with a line for each scenario, labeled by the sims' labels. Here is the outbreak with 90% of people immune, against 85%:

```{python}
scenarios = {
    '85% immune': ss.Sim(make_measles(0.85), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0),
    '90% immune': ss.Sim(make_measles(0.90), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

With more people susceptible (R = 2.3 at the start, instead of 1.5), the outbreak is much faster and larger. The many runs of a stochastic model are plotted as their median at each time point, with a band holding 95% of the runs; `lines=True` plots every run instead:

```{python}
runs = ss.parallel(sim.new(solver='binomial'), n_runs=10)
runs.plot('measles.I')                # The median and the range of 95% of the runs
runs.plot('measles.I', lines=True)    # Every run
```

The band says how much chance alone changes the course of the outbreak: the date of the peak varies by several weeks between runs.

Plots mark when interventions act: a dashed line at each round of a delivery, and a shaded span from the start to the stop of an `ss.modify()` or of routine delivery. In a comparison, the marks of every scenario are gray, and those of one scenario alone are in its color, so it is clear which change made which difference. Deliveries on an event or a condition are not marked, since they have no fixed times; `show_interventions=False` leaves the marks out. Here, in the town with 85% immune, a campaign that vaccinates half of everyone on 15 January or on 1 February:

```{python}
def campaign(date=None):
    vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, when=date, coverage=0.5) if date else None
    return ss.Sim(make_measles(0.85), interventions=vaccination, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)

msim = ss.parallel({'No campaign': campaign(), '15 January': campaign('2025-01-15'), '1 February': campaign('2025-02-01')})
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

A campaign two weeks into the outbreak brings R from 2.3 down to 1.2, so the outbreak smolders rather than taking off, and about 3,100 people are infected by July rather than 12,900 (though it is not quite over); one two weeks later, as cases rise steeply, still prevents more than half of the infections (about 5,700). `sim.diseases.measles.Rt()` gives R over each run (see [Writing models](building_writing.qmd#the-reproduction-number)).

See [Scenarios](running_scenarios.qmd) for running scenarios and many runs, and [Results of many runs](#results-of-many-runs) for their summaries.

## Styles and fonts

Starsim's plots use its own style by default (`'starsim'`), with the Mulish font that comes with Starsim. A plot can use another with `style=`: `'simple'`, `'fancy'`, or any of Matplotlib's styles, such as `'seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid'` or `'ggplot'`. Fonts are given with `font=`: Starsim also comes with Raleway and Rosario, and `font='sans-serif'` uses Matplotlib's default font. Here is the same plot in the default style and in Matplotlib's `'ggplot'` style:

```{python}
sim.plot('measles.I', figsize=(6, 3))
sim.plot('measles.I', figsize=(6, 3), style='ggplot', font='sans-serif')
```

To change the style of every plot, set it once: `ss.options(style='simple')`. To use Starsim's style for plots of your own, use `ss.style()` in a `with` block (below).

## Saving figures

Outside Jupyter (in a script), a plotting function returns the figure, which is saved with Matplotlib's `savefig()`. Give `do_show=False` so that the figure isn't shown first:

```python
fig = sim.plot(do_show=False)
fig.savefig('measles.png', dpi=150)
```

In Jupyter, a plotting function shows the figure and returns nothing, so that the figure isn't displayed twice. `filename=` saves the figure as well as showing it, and `do_show=False` returns the figure without showing it, to change or save it yourself:

```{python}
sim.plot('measles.I', filename='my-measles.png') # Shown, and saved

fig = sim.plot('measles.I', do_show=False) # Returned, not shown
fig.savefig('my-measles.png', dpi=150)
```

Outside Jupyter, the figure is always returned, and shown as `ss.options.show` says (`ss.options(show=False)` stops the plotting functions from showing it). A figure or axes given with `fig=` or `ax=` are yours, so they are not shown (unless `do_show=True`), and more can be plotted into them: `fig = res1.plot(do_show=False)`, then `res2.plot(fig=fig)`. `log=True` gives the y axes a log scale.

## Falling back to Matplotlib

Anything Starsim doesn't plot can be plotted with Matplotlib from the results, since a result is an array with its time points (`res.I.timevec`, `res.I.values`). Starsim's plotting functions also take `fig=` (to plot into an existing figure) and `ax=` (for a single result, into existing axes), so that a figure of your own can mix the two. `ss.style()` applies Starsim's style (or another) to plots of your own, and `sc.commaticks()` from [Sciris](https://docs.sciris.org/) puts commas in large numbers on an axis. Here the share of people who have been infected (the attack rate) is compared with the share still susceptible, in the two scenarios:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

with ss.style():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
    for label, scenario in scenarios.items():
        res = scenario.results.measles
        attack = res.infection.cum / 100_000 # Infected since the start, as a share of everyone
        ax.plot(res.infection.timevec, attack, label=label)
    ax.set_title('Share of people infected since the start')
    ax.set_ylabel('Share of the population')
    ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
    ax.legend()
    plt.show()
```

The results are also tables: `res.to_df()` gives a dataframe, which can be plotted with pandas or seaborn, and `msim.to_df(quantiles=[0.025, 0.5, 0.975])` gives the quantiles of every result across runs, in long form, for a plotting library that works with tables.

## Other plots

Besides results over time, Starsim draws maps: a result stratified by place, drawn on a map of its places at several times or as an animation (`res.prevalence.map()`), and a map of the places themselves, colored by any value for each place (`geo.plot(values=...)`, e.g. a summary of a result by place); see [Places and data](populations_places.qmd). It also plots a disease's diagram, the people and their contacts, distributions, fits, and how long a run took; the [appendix](#appendix-every-plotting-function) lists every plotting function.

## Pitfalls

- **The flow at a time point is the step that starts there.** The peak in infections dated 10 March is the infections during 10 March, with daily steps, and the weekly total dated 3 March is the week from 3 March. Data dated by the end of each period ("week ending") needs its dates moved back by one period to be compared.
- **A ratio is not a mean over groups.** Use `res.prevalence.select(age='65+')`, not the mean of the prevalence in each group.
- **Agents' results are scaled.** With each agent standing for several people, counts are multiplied by that number when the run ends; a count read in the middle of a run is in agents (see [Branching and rescaling](running_branching.qmd)).

## Further reading

- [pandas: 10 minutes to pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/10min.html): working with the tables that `to_df()` gives
- [pandas: time series and date functionality](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/timeseries.html): resampling and dates, as `to_series()` gives them
- [Matplotlib: style sheets reference](https://matplotlib.org/stable/gallery/style_sheets/style_sheets_reference.html): the styles that `style=` accepts
- [Seaborn](https://seaborn.pydata.org/): statistical plots from tables, such as those `to_df()` gives
- [Ten simple rules for better figures](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003833): advice on making figures that communicate

## Appendix: everything a result can do

The methods and properties of a result (`ss.Result`), with the first paragraph of each one's description, listed from the code; a result also does what a NumPy array does (indexing, arithmetic, `sum()`, `max()`). See [`ss.Result`](../api/results.qmd) for the details.

```{python}
import inspect

internal = ['disp', 'to_str', 'update'] # Used by Starsim itself
for name, attr in ss.Result.__dict__.items():
    if name.startswith('_') or name in internal or not isinstance(attr, (property, type(lambda: 0))):
        continue
    doc = ' '.join((attr.__doc__ or '').split('\n\n')[0].split()) # The first paragraph, on one line
    print(name.ljust(16), doc)
```

## Appendix: every plotting function

Every plotting function takes the settings of `ss.plot_args()` (`figsize`, `filename`, `do_show`, `style`, and the others above).

| Plot | What it shows | See |
|---|---|---|
| `sim.plot()` | The results of a sim, each in its own axes, with any data | [Plotting a sim](#plotting-a-sim) |
| `module.plot()` | The results of one module, its states together by default | [Plotting a sim](#plotting-a-sim) |
| `res.plot()` | One result (one line per column or group), or across runs, the median and a 95% interval | [Plotting results](#plotting-results) |
| `res.map()` | A result stratified by place, on a map of its places, at several times or as an animation | [Places and data](populations_places.qmd) |
| `geo.plot()` | A map of the places of a geography, colored by a value for each place if given (`values=`) | [Places and data](populations_places.qmd) |
| `msim.plot()` | The results of many runs or scenarios: the median and a 95% interval of each, or every run (`lines=True`) | [Comparing scenarios and runs](#comparing-scenarios-and-runs) |
| `msim.plot_each()` | Each run on its own time axis, for sims with different time points | [Scenarios](running_scenarios.qmd) |
| `msim.branching.plot()` | For a branching process, the distribution of the chains' sizes (and, as agents, their lengths in generations) | [Branching and rescaling](running_branching.qmd) |
| `disease.diagram()`, `sim.diagram()` | A declared disease's states and transitions (or every disease's, and how they act on each other), drawn; `diagram('text')` gives a Mermaid flowchart | [Writing models](building_writing.qmd#equations-diagram-and-transitions) |
| `sim.people.plot()`, `sim.people.plot_ages()` | Agents' attributes, as histograms; the age pyramid | [People and demographics](populations_people.qmd) |
| `network.plot()` | The contacts of a network of agents | [Mixing](populations_mixing.qmd) |
| `dist.plot_hist()` | Draws from a distribution, as a histogram | [Distributions](mechanics_distributions.qmd) |
| `fit.plot()` | A fit: the data against the model before and after fitting, and with `residuals=True`, the differences | [Fitting a model](calibration_fitting.qmd), [Fit diagnostics](calibration_diagnostics.qmd) |
| `comparison.plot()` | Each model's fit and prediction against held-out data, from `ss.fitting.compare_models()` | [Fit diagnostics](calibration_diagnostics.qmd) |
| `infection_log.plot()` | When each agent was infected, from the `ss.infection_log` analyzer (and `animate()`, as an animation) | [Analyzers](interventions_analyzers.qmd#the-infection-log) |
| `icer.plot()`, `icer.plot_ceac()` | The cost-effectiveness plane, and the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve, from `ssl.econ.ICER` | [Health economics](library_econ.qmd) |
| `sim.loop.plot()` | The order in which modules are called in each step | [From declaration to run](architecture_run.qmd) |
| `sim.loop.plot_cpu()` | The time spent on each event of the loop (each module's methods) during a run | [Debugging](running_debugging.qmd) |
